competency.competency_text: Understand the roles, functions, and significance of constitutional institutions.

assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can describe the role Fundamental Rights play as enforceable institutional guarantees within the constitutional structure.
assessment_items.question_text: The chapter describes Fundamental Rights as 'binding promises rather than mere guidelines.' What institutional feature makes a Fundamental Right different from a policy goal in the Constitution?

options.label: A
options.text: Fundamental Rights apply only to government officials, while ordinary citizens are covered by regular law.

options.label: B
options.text: Fundamental Rights are more important than other constitutional provisions because they appear in the earlier parts of the Constitution.

options.label: C
options.text: Fundamental Rights are permanent and can never be amended or changed by Parliament under any circumstances.

options.label: D
options.text: Fundamental Rights can be enforced through courts — if a citizen's right is violated, they can approach a court and receive a remedy, making the guarantee judicially actionable.

what_each_option_reveals.B: Confuses constitutional significance with textual ordering — position in the document is not the source of a right's binding force; this reflects a surface-level reading rather than understanding of institutional function.
what_each_option_reveals.A: Inverts the chapter's logic — Fundamental Rights protect all citizens against violations, including those by the state and government actors; this misconception may arise from confusing rights with professional obligations.
what_each_option_reveals.C: Overextends the binding nature of Fundamental Rights to mean unamendable — the chapter describes an amendment process and notes the Constitution has been amended; Fundamental Rights are enforceable but not frozen.

competency.competency_text: Understand the roles, functions, and significance of constitutional institutions.

assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can describe the function Directive Principles serve as policy-guiding instruments within the constitutional order.

options.label: A
options.text: Article 38 and Article 47, because both address the social and economic well-being of citizens — Article 38 directs the government to work for social, political, and economic justice, while Article 47 directs it to raise the standard of living and improve public health.

options.label: B
options.text: Article 41 and Article 48-A, because both can be enforced by citizens in court if the government fails to act on them.

options.label: C
options.text: Article 44 and Article 38, because both were originally part of Fundamental Rights before being moved to the DPSP section.

options.label: D
options.text: Article 44 and Article 49, because both deal with how citizens should treat each other in personal and cultural matters.

assessment_items.visual_stimulus:
DPSP Article | What it directs | Category
Article 38 | Government to work for social, political, and economic justice | Social and economic justice
Article 41 | Right to work, education, and public assistance in certain cases | Welfare
Article 44 | Uniform Civil Code for citizens | Legal uniformity
Article 47 | Raise the level of nutrition, standard of living, and improve public health | Public health and welfare
Article 48-A | Protect and improve the environment and safeguard forests and wildlife | Environment
Article 49 | Protect monuments and places of national importance | Cultural heritage
assessment_items.inclusivity: The table is provided to reduce memory load and allow students to focus on classification reasoning rather than recall of article content.

what_each_option_reveals.D: Misclassifies Article 44 (Uniform Civil Code, a legal-structural provision) and Article 49 (protection of monuments, a heritage provision) as personal conduct directives — confuses the domain each article addresses.
what_each_option_reveals.B: Applies the Fundamental Rights concept (justiciability) to DPSP — the chapter is explicit that citizens cannot go to court if the government fails to pursue DPSP, so this option reflects a direct conceptual confusion between the two constitutional categories.
what_each_option_reveals.C: Fabricates a constitutional history not present in the chapter — neither article was previously a Fundamental Right; this tests whether students are importing incorrect information or reading the table accurately.

competency.competency_text: Identify constitutional mechanisms that address inequality and ensure inclusion.

assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can identify which Fundamental Rights directly address specific forms of inequality or exclusion.
assessment_items.question_text: Riya is denied admission to a school because of her caste. Meena, aged 8, has never attended school because her family could not access one. Priya was forced to work without pay. Which row of the table correctly identifies the Fundamental Right each person can invoke?

options.label: A
options.text: Riya: Right against Exploitation; Meena: Right to Freedom (Article 21); Priya: Right to Equality (Article 14).

options.label: B
options.text: Riya: Right to Education (Article 21-A); Meena: Right against Exploitation; Priya: Right to Equality (Article 14).

options.label: C
options.text: Riya: Right to Equality (Article 14); Meena: Right to Education (Article 21-A); Priya: Right against Exploitation.

options.label: D
options.text: Riya: Right to Freedom (Article 21); Meena: Right to Equality (Article 14); Priya: Right to Education (Article 21-A).

assessment_items.inclusivity: The three-person scenario allows students to approach the question through relatable situations rather than abstract article matching.

what_each_option_reveals.D: Confuses the Right to Freedom (general liberty provision) with the Right to Equality (anti-discrimination provision) for Riya's caste-based denial — and misapplies the Right to Education to forced labour rather than educational access.
what_each_option_reveals.A: Assigns the Right against Exploitation to caste discrimination — conflating 'exploitation' with 'discrimination'; and assigns the Right to Freedom to lack of educational access, showing a generalised rather than specific understanding of each right.
what_each_option_reveals.B: Assigns the Right to Education to Riya's caste-discrimination scenario and the Right against Exploitation to Meena's educational access scenario — a complete cross-mapping that suggests the student knows the article names but has not connected them to the specific inequalities each addresses.

competency.competency_text: Identify constitutional mechanisms that address inequality and ensure inclusion.

assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can identify which Directive Principles are designed to reduce socio-economic inequality and promote inclusion.
assessment_items.question_text: A researcher is studying which DPSP articles were specifically designed to reduce socio-economic inequality. Which combination of articles should the researcher prioritise, and why?

options.label: A
options.text: Articles 38 and 41 — Article 38 directs the state to reduce social and economic inequalities, and Article 41 establishes the goal of securing the right to work and assistance for those in need, both targeting the most vulnerable sections of society.

options.label: B
options.text: Articles 41 and 44 — both articles can be enforced in court, making them the strongest tools for citizens facing economic hardship.

options.label: C
options.text: Articles 44 and 49 — a Uniform Civil Code ensures legal equality, and protecting national monuments ensures all citizens have equal access to heritage, together reducing inequality.

options.label: D
options.text: Articles 48-A and 49 — protecting the environment and monuments ensures that natural and cultural resources are available to all citizens equally, which directly reduces inequality.

what_each_option_reveals.C: Overstretches the meaning of 'reducing inequality' to cover legal uniformity (Article 44) and heritage access (Article 49) — which do not primarily address socio-economic inequality in the chapter's framing; reflects a broad-brush application of the concept.
what_each_option_reveals.D: Applies an indirect-access logic (environmental and cultural resources available to all) rather than identifying articles directly targeting socio-economic disadvantage — a creative but off-target interpretation of the chapter's content.
what_each_option_reveals.B: Reintroduces the Fundamental Rights misconception (court-enforceability) into DPSP — which the chapter explicitly states DPSP do not carry; also misidentifies Article 44 as relevant to economic hardship.

competency.competency_text: Understand how India's cultural unity in diversity is expressed as a constitutional value.

assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can illustrate how India's tradition of embracing diverse perspectives became a foundational constitutional value.
assessment_items.question_text: The chapter says that 'acceptance of diverse points of view' and the concept of vasudhaiva kutumbakam are part of India's civilisational heritage that found their way into the Constitution. Which constitutional feature is the most direct expression of this tradition?

options.label: A
options.text: The amendment process, because allowing the Constitution to change over time means it can adapt to new cultural practices as they emerge.

options.label: B
options.text: The Fundamental Duty to defend the country, because protecting India ensures that its diverse traditions survive against external threats.

options.label: C
options.text: The Secular character of the Constitution, which ensures the government treats all religious beliefs and practices with equal respect and there is no official religion — directly institutionalising the acceptance of diverse views within a single nation.

options.label: D
options.text: The three-tier system of government, because having local, state, and central levels allows each region's cultural diversity to be represented at its own level.

what_each_option_reveals.B: Connects the duty to defend the country to cultural preservation through an indirect chain — the connection is real at a general level but does not reflect the chapter's specific argument about civilisational traditions of diversity becoming constitutional values; it is a thematic leap rather than a traced connection.
what_each_option_reveals.D: Attributes diversity-representation to the three-tier structure — which is a governance efficiency and federal design feature, not the chapter's account of how civilisational acceptance of diverse views became constitutional; conflates structural federalism with cultural pluralism.
what_each_option_reveals.A: Attributes the tradition of accepting diverse views to the amendment process — which is a procedural feature about constitutional change over time, not about the coexistence of diverse perspectives within the Constitution; this confuses two different senses of 'accepting diversity'.

competency.competency_text: Understand how India's cultural unity in diversity is expressed as a constitutional value.

assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can illustrate how India's tradition of embracing diverse perspectives became a foundational constitutional value.
assessment_items.question_text: A teacher says: 'India's Constitution is not just a legal document — it is also a cultural one.' Which evidence from the chapter best supports this claim?

options.label: A
options.text: The Constitution borrows from the constitutions of France, Ireland, the USA, and other countries, showing that it is shaped by global culture rather than only Indian legal traditions.

options.label: B
options.text: The Constitution has 25 parts and 12 schedules, showing that it is comprehensive enough to address every aspect of Indian cultural life.

options.label: C
options.text: The Constitution requires all important officials to take an oath, which is a cultural ritual that predates written law in many societies.

options.label: D
options.text: The Constitution was handwritten by calligrapher Prem Behari Narain Raizada and illustrated by Nandalal Bose with scenes from Indian history ranging from Mohenjo-daro to the freedom movement, treating it as a cultural artefact alongside a legal text.

what_each_option_reveals.A: Conflates global borrowing (a constitutional design strategy) with cultural identity — the argument that foreign influences make the document 'cultural' misunderstands the claim; this option confuses the origin of ideas with their cultural expression.
what_each_option_reveals.B: Uses the size and comprehensiveness of the Constitution as evidence for its cultural character — which conflates scope with cultural meaning; having many parts does not make a document a cultural artefact.
what_each_option_reveals.C: The oath argument stretches 'cultural ritual' to cover a constitutional procedure — while oaths have cultural dimensions, the chapter's specific claim about the Constitution as a cultural document is best evidenced by the artistic commission of Raizada and Nandalal Bose, not by the oath provision.
